Dear Mr. Kramer:
Our office received your request for an opinion submitted on behalf of the Board of
Commissioners for Franklin Parish Hospital Service District #1 (“District”) concerning
the sale of accounts receivable. Consistent with our discussion regarding your request,
the accounts at issue range in amounts from twenty dollars to around twenty thousand
dollars. Your request states that “all legal avenues have been exhausted” in pursuing
collection of these accounts, and that private corporate entities have expressed an
interest in the purchase of these accounts receivable.
In light of the above, you have specifically asked:
(1) Whether a political subdivision, such as the District, may sell accounts receivable
to a private entity;
(2) If the answer to the first question is in the affirmative, is the procedure for selling
accounts receivable the same as that which must be followed for selling surplus
movable property, i.e., declaration of surplus, publication, bid/auction, etc.; and
(3) If the answer to the second question is in the affirmative, can the accounts be
sold in a bulk transaction or must they be sold one account at a time?
As a starting point, we consider the ability of the District to dispose of property. The
powers of a hospital service district are described in La. R.S. 46:1060, which provides:
Any hospital service district thus created and named by any police jury or
any parish in the state shall constitute a body corporate in law with all the
powers of a corporation, shall have perpetual existence, shall have the

OPINION 13-0061
Mr. Blake Kramer
Page 2
power and right to incur debts and contract obligations, to sue and be
sued, and to do and perform any and all acts in its corporate capacity and
its corporate name necessary and proper for the carrying out of the
objects and purposes for which the hospital service district was created.
Such hospital service district shall have the right and power of
expropriating property for the purpose of acquiring land for any purpose
that it may find necessary in the operation of a hospital service district and
may require by donation or purchase, any existing hospital facility in the
district. It shall also have the power and authority to acquire any and all
necessary equipment and buildings for the purpose of performing the
objects for which it is formed, and shall own all sites and physical facilities
which are acquired either by donation, purchase, expropriation, exchange
and otherwise in full ownership.
Pursuant to La. R.S. 46:1060 a hospital service district is authorized “to do and perform
any and all acts in its corporate capacity and its corporate name necessary and proper
for the carrying out of the objects and purposes for which the hospital service district
was created.” Such acts would seem to include the sale of property or assets that are
determined by the District to be no longer needed for public purposes or which are
diminishing in value.
Your first question specifically asks whether it is permissible for the District to sell
accounts receivable, accounts which the District has claimed to have “exhausted all
legal avenues to collect.” In La. Atty. Gen. Op. No. 02-0104, our office was asked
whether LSU Health Care Services Division could negotiate a sale of uncollected and
apparently uncollectible accounts receivable. LSU contracted with a commercial
collection agency who attempted without success to collect the accounts and LSU
Health Care Services Division then declared such accounts as “uncollectible.” Id. This
office concluded that we were unaware of any provision of law that would prohibit the
sale of such accounts “as long as the Health Care Services Division has exhausted all
reasonable avenues for the collection of these accounts and as long as the Health Care
services Division will receive payment for the accounts commensurate with their value.”1
Id.
Whether the accounts at issue in your opinion request should be qualified as
“uncollectible” or whether the District has exhausted all reasonable avenues for the
collection of such accounts is a fact specific inquiry, and our office does not serve as a
fact-finder. We do, however, note that before the District could contemplate the sale of
any accounts receivable, the District must give careful and deliberate consideration of
each specific account, including examining the District’s own efforts to collect on the
account. While your request states that the District has “exhausted all legal avenues to
collect” these past due accounts, your letter did not include a description of such efforts.
1 Please note that the requestor in La. Atty. Gen. Op. No. 02-0104 indicated that “according to the
Accounting Principles Board, accounts that are more than six months old are worth fifty to sixty cents on
the dollar, while those that are more than one year old are worth about thirty cents on the dollar.”

Mr. Blake Kramer
Page 3
In considering the relationship between debts owed to a public body and La. Const. art.
VII, §14, our office has previously stated that this constitutional provision requires public
bodies exercise reasonable means to recover debts owed to the public body.2
Reasonable means must be determined by the agency on a case-by-case basis and on
sound business practices and principles.3 As described by La. Atty. Gen. Op. No. 02-
0104, such reasonable means may include a public body entering into a professional
services contract with a third party for debt collection services.4
For the reasons described above, the District, and not our office, is in the best position
to consider what reasonable collection efforts should be undertaken by the District
before declaring the accounts “uncollectible” and, further, what amount would represent
a fair value for such accounts. However, consistent with La. Atty. Gen. Op. No. 02-
0104, our office is of the opinion that there is nothing prohibiting the sale of
“uncollectible” accounts receivable provided prior reasonable efforts are made to collect
on such accounts, and the District receives payment for the accounts commensurate
with their value.
Should the District conclude that reasonable collection efforts have been made to
collect on the accounts receivable such that the accounts are properly classified as
“uncollectible,” the question then turns to the correct procedure for disposing of such
property.
As stated above, the revised statutes do not specify an exact procedure which a
hospital service district must follow in disposing of “uncollectible” accounts receivable.
However, pursuant to La.Const. art. VII, §14, the District should follow the same
publication and notice requirements that it would follow if it were disposing of surplus
movable property.5 Thus, the District should declare at a public meeting that the
accounts qualify as “uncollectible” and that the accounts will, after notice, be offered for
sale to the highest bidder. The District should fix a minimum price which would reflect
the fair value of the accounts and which may be obtained through an appraisal of the
accounts. Any sale must be such that the District receives payment for the accounts
commensurate with their value.
In response to your third question, we see nothing prohibiting the sale of the accounts in
bulk, rather than one account at a time, if such method is deemed by the District and the
District’s Director to be the method which would generate the most interest and income
for the property.

action to be made known, and in our estimate, generates the most interest to get the best price for the
property sought to be sold.” Attached, please find copies of these opinions.

Mr. Blake Kramer
Page 4
In conclusion, it is the opinion of this office that the District may sell accounts receivable
to a private entity if such accounts are determined by the District to be “uncollectible” at
a public meeting. Should the district classify the accounts accordingly, then such
accounts should be sold to the highest bidder only after obtaining an appraisal of the
accounts representing their fair market value, setting a minimum price, and giving public
notice of the intended sale. Further, there is nothing which prohibits the District from
selling the accounts in bulk, rather than one at a time, should the District determine this
method of sale is the method which would generate the most interest and income.
We hope that this opinion has adequately addressed the legal issues you have raised.
If our office can be of any further assistance, please do not hesitate to contact us.
With best regards,
JAMES D. “BUDDY” CALDWELL
ATTORNEY GENERAL
